clinicalPearls: Presents with deep subcutaneous nodules or plaques, often on the limbs and trunk, that clinically resemble a panniculitis
Systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and weight loss are common, and a subset develop an associated haemophagocytic syndrome that dominates the clinical picture
By definition the neoplastic infiltrate is confined to subcutaneous fat, rimming individual adipocytes, without dermal or epidermal involvement
Tumour cells are cytotoxic T-lymphocytes of the alpha-beta lineage, typically CD8-positive and betaF1-positive, with expression of cytotoxic granule proteins
It must be separated from primary cutaneous gamma-delta T-cell lymphoma, which involves dermis and epidermis, is more aggressive, and carries a worse prognosis
An overlap exists with lupus erythematosus panniculitis, and the two can be difficult to distinguish or may coexist
In the absence of haemophagocytic syndrome the course is often relatively indolent
reference.pathophysiology: Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma is a cytotoxic T-cell neoplasm derived from alpha-beta T-lymphocytes that selectively infiltrates subcutaneous adipose tissue. The malignant cells characteristically surround individual fat cells, producing a lobular panniculitis-like pattern with fat necrosis and karyorrhexis while sparing the overlying dermis and epidermis. Cytotoxic activity and cytokine release can drive macrophage activation, precipitating a haemophagocytic syndrome that accounts for much of the disease's morbidity. Some cases arise on a background of, or overlap with, autoimmune disease, blurring the boundary with lupus panniculitis.
additionalDifferentials: Erythema nodosum and other reactive panniculitides
Other cutaneous T-cell lymphomas with subcutaneous spread
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional skin biopsy sampling subcutaneous fat with immunohistochemistry (CD8, betaF1, cytotoxic markers)
Assessment of the T-cell receptor lineage to exclude a gamma-delta phenotype
Ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, and blood counts to screen for haemophagocytic syndrome
Autoimmune serology to evaluate for lupus panniculitis overlap
Cross-sectional imaging and bone marrow examination if systemic disease is suspected
redFlags: Development of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with cytopenias, high ferritin, and organ dysfunction
Rapid dissemination or transformation to a more aggressive phenotype
Extensive ulcerating disease suggesting a gamma-delta lymphoma rather than SPTCL
Systemic deterioration with high fever and multi-organ involvement
reference.prognosis: Without haemophagocytic syndrome the prognosis is generally favourable and disease may be controlled with immunosuppression or systemic therapy, but an associated haemophagocytic syndrome markedly worsens outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the lesions as benign panniculitis and delaying biopsy
Failing to distinguish SPTCL from the more aggressive gamma-delta cutaneous lymphoma
Confusing the condition with lupus panniculitis, which it can closely resemble or coexist with
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
